main_point.en: We can expect rejection for following Jesus.

christ_connection.en: Hundreds of years before Jesus was born, the prophet Isaiah wrote of God’s plan to send someone to bring good news and redeem His captive people. Jesus proclaimed that He was the fulfillment of Isaiah’s prophecy—the promised Messiah. Jesus was rejected by the people, but it was through that very rejection—the cross—that He provided redemption from sin.

content.en: 16 And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. 17 And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written, 18 “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, 19 to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.” 20 And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. 21 And he began to say to them, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” 22 And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, “Is not this Joseph’s son?” 23 And he said to them, “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ““Physician, heal yourself.” What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.”
Leaders: This week, pray for your students who are struggling with rejection from their friends and peers. Look for ways to encourage them to press on, regardless of what others think.
“Luke indicated that Jesus deliberately chose the following passage to read and thus emphasized Jesus’s messianic consciousness as he began his ministry.”⁷

“Jesus did, in fact, go to these very kinds of people and proclaim, preach, and teach the kingdom of God. The primary means of setting people free in whatever their social or political circumstance is the proclamation of the gospel. But that means the gospel has to be so real a gospel that it addresses people in their social and political position. The gospel cannot be abstracted from the real conditions of the people it addresses. Israel was under Roman occupation. Israel was oppressed. Israel was crushed beneath the heel of the Caesars. And Christ came to them preaching the gospel of the kingdom—not the kingdom of Caesar but of another world. He gave hope to a people broken by the rule of men.”⁸

“Sidon and Syria were Gentile lands and people. Jesus is saying God’s salvation passed over Israel and went to the ‘unclean’ Gentiles. Israel rejected their prophets, but the Gentiles received them and were saved. Now we remember the last words of Isaiah 61: ‘For as the earth produces its growth, and as a garden enables what is sown to spring up, so the Lord GoD will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations’ (v. 11). God always intended to save people from every nation and ethnic group and language group, not just from Israel. As Paul explains in Romans, the Gentiles have been grafted into God’s salvation because the Israelites have been broken off (Rom. 11:17). That is what Jesus preaches here: Israel will be cut off and the Gentiles brought in.”⁹

This passage in Luke displays how Jesus identified Himself both as a prophet and as the Messiah described in Old Testament prophecies. Jesus read from Isaiah 61:1-2, which describes an anointed figure sent by God to bring deliverance, healing, and good news. Jesus identified Himself as this figure when He proclaimed that this Scripture had been fulfilled. Just like many prophets were rejected by their own people, Jesus was also rejected in His hometown of Nazareth. He referenced the stories of Elijah and Elisha to point to what His own ministry would look like. These two Old Testament prophets didn’t show favoritism toward the Israelites but willingly ministered to non-Israelites. Elijah miraculously provided food for a widow and her family in Sidon 4 Kings 17:8-16). Elisha did not cleanse any Israelites of leprosy, but he told Naaman, the commander of the Syrian army, how to be healed (2 Kings 5:1-14). Jesus would also minister to many Gentiles (non-Jews) throughout His ministry, while His own Jewish people frequently rejected Him. Jesus’s audience understood the implications of His teachings: Jewish people would not be the only ones to receive deliverance and healing from God, and they were being accused of rejecting God’s prophets. The angry mob tried to kill Jesus, but He evaded them, perhaps through some supernatural means.

Sometimes in Scripture the term “world” refers to more than the physical planet Earth or the collective human population. In many instances, the term refers to an active and evil spiritual force that is in direct conflict with God and His kingdom. This evil world force operates under Satan’s control (Eph. 2:2; John 14:30), displaying the same self-centeredness and deceit that is found within his character. Christians are called to overcome this world of spiritual evil by faith in the Son of God (1 John 5:4-5).

LORD, HELP US TO FOLLOW YOU FAITHFULLY, EVEN WHEN IT REQUIRES SACRIFICE. THANK YOU FOR COMING TO OUR BROKEN WORLD AND EXPERIENCING REJECTION SO THAT WE CAN BE SAVED. PLEASE HELP OUR STUDENTS SEE THAT YOU ARE WORTHY OF OUR WORSHIP, EVEN IF WE FACE REJECTION FOR IT.

question.en: How do you feel about taking a risk that might result in rejection (1=Super confident; 10=Utterly terrified)?

instructions.en:
These optional activities are designed to help your students interact. You'll find a Discussion Activity and a Cultural Connection, which touches on a relevant topic in today’s teen culture. Each group is different, so adapt these activities to fit your group’s needs. The goal is for students to connect more to the lesson as they connect to the topic and to one another.

SUPPLIES LIST: NONE

Ask the following questions, allowing time for students to share responses:

question.en: When have you been afraid of being rejected? Why do you think we worry so much about being rejected?
How does being rejected impact how we feel about ourselves or others?
Describe a circumstance when being rejected may be a good thing.

content.en: Most of us don’t like the idea of rejection, and we typically try to avoid the risk of being rejected. Jesus knows exactly how being rejected by people feels—even the very people He came to save. Yet this was a part of God’s plan to redeem us. Jesus’s rejection led to His death, but His death and resurrection paved the way for us to be restored to God.

cultural_connection.en: We are surrounded by voices that tell us how we should act, dress, speak, and think if we want people to accept us. We may feel pressure from our family, friends, classmates, or social media to conform to what’s popular to fit in. We want to be well-liked, so much that we compromise our beliefs to avoid rejection. Maybe you go along with the majority opinion, even if it means agreeing with something sinful. Maybe you participate in behavior you know is wrong because you’re more concerned with fitting in than obeying God. We worry that taking a godly stance will cause others to tease us, accuse us of ruining the fun, or label us intolerant or hateful. However, avoiding rejection robs us of living obediently to God’s Word. As Christians, we certainly shouldn’t go out of our way to offend people or cause chaos. We can disagree with others and still show love and respect (Rom. 12:18), even if the world opposes our biblical values. Though we may face rejection, we must be open to talking with people about our Christian convictions in the hope that they will come to know the Lord.

question.en: How did the people in Jesus’s hometown look at Him? Why did they ask if He was Joseph’s son?

answer.en: Jesus preached in His childhood synagogue in Nazareth, a small and insignificant town, where the people likely knew Jesus and His family. Hearing one of their own people claim to be God’s Anointed One astonished them. The Jews had hoped and prayed for the Messiah to come for generations. The prophecy about the Messiah’s birth indicated that He would come from Bethlehem (Mic. 5:2), not Nazareth. Jesus was born in Bethlehem! But His family moved to Nazareth after a short time. Jesus coming from an ordinary town and from an unimportant family made His claims difficult for people to believe.

question.en: Jesus claimed to fulfill Isaiah’s prophecy for the Messiah. How did Jesus display this in His ministry?

answer.en: Jesus demonstrated that He had the power to meet people’s physical and spiritual needs. He proclaimed the good news of the gospel: God sent Him to offer forgiveness of sin and eternal life to everyone through His death and resurrection. He ministered to social outcasts who were labeled sinful or unclean. He healed the sick and disabled, gave sight to the blind, and set people free from demonic oppression. Jesus did all these things by the power and authority God the Father gave to Him, and He welcomed anyone who came to Him in faith.

question.en: Many people had doubts about Jesus. When are you most tempted to doubt who Jesus says He is?

answer.en: We may struggle to trust that Jesus really is the Messiah for several reasons. Our world rejects Jesus and tries to make us doubt our beliefs. We see people walk away from their faith after professing to be Christians for years. Christian leaders fail us; believers in the church hurt us. Sometimes, our circumstances are not what we expect, and we wonder if God has forgotten us or if He is real at all. In these difficult situations, we must remind ourselves of the truth of God’s Word. Broken people are likely to fail us, but Jesus never will. We must place our faith in our holy, perfect Savior and not in sinful, fallen people. Our hearts deceive us and lead us astray (Jer. 17:9), so we must consistently fill our minds with truth. Experiencing doubt or having questions isn’t shameful. Like the man who begged Jesus to help his unbelief (Mark 9:24), we can come to Jesus with our doubts and questions. The best way to combat doubt? Invest in knowing Jesus. When you do, you’ll see His words are true and His character is steady. Jesus loves you; He isn’t waiting to punish you for wrestling with doubt. He will show you compassion and patience as you surrender your doubt to Him.

question.en: What was Jesus’s message to the people of Nazareth? Why were they offended?

answer.en: The people enjoyed Jesus’s message until it contradicted their expectations for the Messiah. While He would perform signs and miracles like Scripture foretold, Jesus would not minister exclusively to the Jewish people. He cared for Samaritans, Roman citizens and officials, and other Gentiles. Jesus explained that His ministry would be like that of Elijah and Elisha, who did not show favoritism toward their own Hebrew people. The Jews of Jesus’s day expected their Messiah to deliver them from Roman oppression, but Jesus was more concerned with providing spiritual deliverance to those in bondage to sin. He made salvation possible for everyone and offered it to everyone—both Jews and Gentiles, which greatly offended those listening to His message, expecting to be exclusive.

question.en: Why do people you know continue to reject Jesus’s message today?

answer.en: Our world is opposed to Jesus and the things of God. The world is temporarily under Satan’s authority, the ruler of this world (John 14:30). As Christians, we are called to proclaim the good news of the gospel so that unbelievers’ eyes may be opened to the truth (2 Cor. 4:4). People accept that God loves us but often reject the gospel because it requires a response that goes against a sinful lifestyle. The gospel calls us to confess our sin, turn from it, and place our lives under Jesus’s lordship. This command goes against our natural, sinful desires: We want to live on our terms and be in control of our lives. Our spiritual blindness prevents us from seeing that our sin leads to death, convincing us to cling to sin rather than to surrender it.

question.en: How did God use Jesus’s rejection to bring salvation to the world? What can this show us about our own rejection?

answer.en: Rejection can have purpose. Jesus’s rejection at home resulted in the crowd trying to hurl Him off a cliff, pointing to His impending death. God used the people’s unbelief and rejection to accomplish our salvation through Jesus’s crucifixion. Jesus said no one would take His life; He would lay it down willingly (John 10:18)—for us. Jesus was rejected so that we could be accepted by God. When we’re rejected because of Jesus, we can lean on the truth that God can use it for His glory.

question.en: Where is the fear of rejection keeping you from obeying God? How does knowing Jesus faced rejection give you strength?

answer.en: Here’s the truth we don’t want to be true: Following Jesus guarantees you won’t always fit in. Your lifestyle won’t make sense. People may stop inviting you to hang out. Your obedience will likely cause tension because walking according to God’s Word will contradict what the world says is normal. Jesus knows what it’s like to live here; He knows how rejection feels because He faced it at the highest level. He wept over His own people, longing to give them peace (Luke 19:41). Even members of His family didn’t believe Him (John 7:5). Ultimately, the very people Jesus came to save killed Him. Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before Him; if we are to keep running in faith, we must fix our eyes on Him (Heb. 12:1-2). Jesus persevered through rejection out of His great love for us—so that we could have a relationship with Him. Remembering the hatred and rejection Jesus faced for us can help us stand strong when we face the same. We will never regret remaining faithful to Jesus; we will regret being unfaithful to avoid rejection.

content.en: In this week’s lesson, we discussed Luke 4:16-30. Jesus read a prophecy about Himself found in Isaiah 61:1-3. This scandalous moment was vital to Jesus’s mission because the words He read were very specific to the sacrifice that He made for our salvation. Let’s break it down. When Jesus said, “The Spirit of the Lord is on me,” He declared that He was the One sent by God as a sacrifice for our sins. When Jesus said that He was sent to “proclaim good news to the poor,” “to proclaim liberty to the captives,” and to “[recover] sight to the blind,” He revealed that He had been sent to set people free from their sins, as well as give sight spiritually and physically. We read about these things in John 9, when Jesus gave sight to a blind man by mixing His spit with dirt to create mud as a healing balm for his eyes. Throughout the Gospels, we see Jesus fulfill Old Testament prophecy, like the one in today’s passage. Why does this matter? If God fulfilled His promise to send a Savior and did, if Jesus did what He said He would do (and He did), then we can absolutely trust God’s promises to us. We can believe the truth of His Word and rest in His faithfulness. Certainly, Jesus fulfilled God’s promise to the Israelites to send someone who would set them free from the consequences of their sin. The better news is that Jesus not only came for the Israelites but for everyone, including you today. Jesus came as a fulfillment of God’s grace to save us all from the destruction of our sins, to liberate us, to give us spiritual sight.

question.en: What are the areas in your life that you struggle with being spiritually blind—unaware of your sin?
How can you trust God on a daily basis, knowing that He is faithful to His promises?

prayer.en: God, thank You for including me as a recipient of Your grace. If I have any spiritual blindness today, please reveal it to me so that I can walk confidently into what You have for me to do.

content.en: Let’s set the stage for today’s Scripture. The widow lived in a place called Zarephath. At first glance, this does not seem significant, but the reality is that Zarephath was a region deeply rooted in worshiping false gods. God’s work wasn’t always evident there, but He wasn’t absent. Now, if you were to read the Scripture again with that knowledge, the significance changes a bit, right? The widow, a worshiper of a false god, fed Elijah, a follower of God, in a time of famine, when food was hard to obtain. Though she didn’t follow Yahweh, she took a big step of faith to feed Elijah the last of her bread. God rewarded her by ensuring that the jar of ingredients to make bread for her son didn’t run out until the drought and famine were over. Something more amazing? When her son later got sick and stopped breathing, Elijah begged for God to restore his life. And God did! As a result, the woman knew God’s words were true. In our main passage this week, Jesus used this story from 1 Kings to show the Jewish listeners that God accepts and takes care of everyone who surrenders to Him, even the ones they despised—the Gentiles. If God called this widow in Zarephath to faith and raised her son from death, then He cares for all people. As outsiders looking in, we can easily judge the Jews for not accepting Gentiles. If you examine your own thoughts and actions about other people, you might find that you also have a hard time accepting someone who is different from you. Have you ever had classmates that you do not like visit your church? How did you react to them being there? Did you invite them to sit with you, or did you give them the cold shoulder? Today’s Scripture shows us that if God can forgive and accept outsiders and the worst of sinners, then we must do the same.

question.en: Is it hard for you to accept people who are different from you? Why or why not?
What part of today’s Scripture can you use as an encouragement to love and welcome everyone into God’s family?

prayer.en: Thank You, God, for forgiving and accepting people from all walks of life. As someone who is also unworthy of Your grace and love, I am so grateful that You give it freely.

content.en: Today’s passage is another story that Jesus referenced in the main lesson this week. When the people heard this story, they were angry—similar to the way we get mad when something good happens to someone we don’t like. Maybe this person used to be mean as a kid, but now he or she is one of the most-liked people at school. Or maybe teachers praise someone else’s work and overlook your hard work. What does it reveal about your heart when you feel anger toward someone in this situation? Well, in most cases we feel jealousy, and though we don’t like admitting it, jealousy is a sin. When you're jealous of what someone else has, you think you’re missing out on getting it for yourself. The truth is that God has enough love and grace for everyone. When He heals or blesses someone else, He doesn’t take from you to bless them. Jesus used the example in today’s passage to reveal to the people of Galilee that their hearts were rooted in prideful sin. If you were there listening to Jesus, would you agree with the crowd’s feelings? Romans 2:11 reminds us that God does not choose favorites. We are all made in His image Gen. 1:27), and He desires to take care of us. He works all things for our good and His glory when we turn to Him (Rom. 8:28). You can rest in your situation today, fully trusting that God is taking care of you in the same way that He is taking care of those around you. If you struggle with jealousy, repent and ask God to help you be excited for the ways God blesses, accepts, and transforms others for His glory.

question.en: What makes you jealous of other people?
How often do you pray for the good of someone you struggle to accept?

prayer.en: Thank You, God, that Your grace is sufficient for everyone and You do not choose favorites. Please forgive me for the times that I am jealous of others. Help me feel joy when You bless others.

content.en: Jesus’s words in today’s passage are a difficult reminder: The darkness of the world is at war with the Light inside of you—with Jesus. The world rejected Jesus when He was on earth. As Christians, we are the dwelling place for the Holy Spirit of God, so we know the world will sometimes reject us too. The good news is that you will be okay—more than okay. In a world full of social media presence and acceptance, that statement feels countercultural. Your feeds are filled with “influencers” telling you what to buy, what style to mimic or filters to use, with a promise of guaranteed acceptance and praise from your peers. This promise of acceptance is difficult to ignore; most of us desire acceptance from the people we are around every day. We're easily discouraged when we don’t fit in. The reality for Christians is that we are called to be in the world but not a part of the world. God wants us to be present and to make an impact, but He doesn’t want us to become wrapped up in what matters to the world. The good news is that God is on our side. He accepts us and loves us! If you look back at John 15:16, Jesus explained that though we didn’t naturally choose Him, He chose us. He made this statement right before saying His followers would be rejected by the world. Jesus wanted His followers to know that we are chosen by the One who matters the most. Let this be an encouragement to you today, as you go into the world and live for God. People won't always like or agree with your choices. The Light within you may offend those living in darkness, but go—shine in the dark world. You’re already loved and accepted by God.

question.en: How have you recently been living for God instead of the world?
When have you looked for acceptance from the world instead of seeking to please God? What was the result?

prayer.en: God, I want to honor You with my words and actions today. If that comes with the cost of not being accepted by everyone, please remind me that I will be okay.

content.en: Isaiah prophesied that the world would despise and reject Jesus. Jesus came to earth fully aware of what He would endure, yet He came for us anyway. Jesus had no beauty that we should desire Him, and He was born into a poor family. The question is not if we would be in the crowd of those who rejected Jesus, but how many times have we been in the crowd protesting against Him? Judging other people for rejecting Jesus is easy—forgetting that we sometimes reject Him as well with our lifestyle, our words, our actions, our priorities. Sin looks fun, so you give in just one time. Your parents don’t seem to understand your life, so you lash out at them in disrespect. A friend makes an inappropriate joke, and because you want to fit in, you laugh when you should stay quiet or walk away. We rebel against God and give in to temptations that don’t honor Him. Paul urged Timothy to “flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart” 2 Tim. 2:22). Make a commitment to be aware of your thoughts and actions so that you can turn—so that you can flee—from temptations instead of getting as close to the line as possible. Before Jesus left earth, He said that He was sending a Helper for all who follow Him. That helper is the Holy Spirit, who dwells within everyone who believes and calls on the Lord for salvation. You are not alone in your decision to walk away from the crowd; the Holy Spirit goes with you when you face rejection from the world.

question.en: What sin do you hold on to so that you stay part of the crowd and avoid rejection? What will it take for you to turn from it?
Scripture says to flee from sin. What do you do to keep from falling into sin? In what ways are you trying to get close to sin instead of running from it?

prayer.en: Father, please forgive me for all the times I have been a part of the crowd that rejected Your Son. Thank You for Your love and Your grace. Help me honor You with my words and actions.
